analysis.one_liner: Overhauls credit reporting to help people fix errors, get free scores, and keep bad credit from costing them jobs.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have overhauled credit reporting rules for about 200 million consumers, was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in September 2017 and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for the credit reporting industry. It would make credit bureaus genuinely investigate disputes instead of rubber-stamping lender answers, let consumers appeal those decisions, and shorten how long bad marks stay on credit reports. It would ban employers from checking credit for most hiring decisions, remove settled medical and student loan debts from reports, and help victims of identity theft, fraud, and predatory lenders clean up their records. It would also require the three big credit bureaus — Equifax, TransUnion, and Experian — to give free credit scores with free annual reports, let consumers freeze their credit for free, and ban the misleading marketing of credit monitoring subscriptions that regulators had just fined the bureaus for. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would get authority to oversee credit scoring models and cap fees bureaus charge consumers.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose credit reports contain errors — the Consumer Bureau found roughly one in four reports has a potentially material error — plus people with medical debt, defaulted private student loans, or damaged credit from job loss, fraud, or abusive relationships. Anyone would gain from free credit scores, faster error corrections, credit freezes, and an end to credit checks in most hiring decisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers with credit report errors or blemishes

how_it_helps.text: Gives consumers a new right to appeal when a credit bureau's investigation of a disputed item does not fix the problem, and requires bureaus to conduct real, independent reinvestigations with trained staff instead of rubber-stamping the lender's answer.

Bans the use of credit reports in most hiring decisions, ending a practice that punishes people whose credit was damaged by job loss, medical bills, or divorce — factors the bill's findings show do not predict job performance.

Requires removal of negative marks from private student loan defaults for borrowers who demonstrate a history of repayment, and provides credit restoration for people defrauded by for-profit schools or predatory mortgage lenders.

Restricts medical collections on credit reports and requires them to be removed once paid, addressing the Consumer Bureau's finding that medical debt can knock 10 to 22 points off scores even for people who otherwise pay their bills on time.

Shortens how long most negative information stays on reports, gives free credit scores with free annual reports, and requires mortgage, auto, and student lenders to show consumers the exact reports and scores used before they sign.

Provides free credit freezes for minors and vulnerable consumers, free credit monitoring for identity theft victims, and removes fraudulent inquiries and accounts caused by identity theft or domestic financial abuse.

Bans misleading marketing of credit scores and automatic-renewal subscription traps that the Consumer Bureau had just fined Equifax, TransUnion, and Experian for in 2017, and gives the CFPB power to cap fees on consumer credit products.

analysis.who_pays: Credit bureaus and data furnishers — banks, lenders, collectors — would bear the cost of keeping records, retraining dispute staff in the US, issuing more notices, and giving away scores and freezes that are now paid products. Employers would lose credit checks as a screening tool.

drawbacks.text: Shortening the time adverse information stays on credit reports and requiring removal of paid or settled debts makes it harder for lenders and landlords to see a full repayment history, which could lead lenders to price risk less precisely or tighten credit for some borrowers.

The bill would impose significant new operating costs on credit bureaus, lenders, and debt collectors — trained US-based dispute staff, record retention, notices before reporting negative information, and free scores, freezes, and monitoring — and some of those costs could be passed on through fees or tighter lending standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to ordinary people would be large and concrete — faster, real investigations of credit errors, an end to credit checks as a job barrier, medical debt and fraud damage removed from reports, and free scores and freezes — while the costs fall on credit bureaus, debt collectors, and lenders, not on consumers. The strongest good-faith objection is that tighter rules and shorter reporting windows could make lenders more cautious and credit slightly more expensive or harder to get for some borrowers, and new mandates on furnishers and CRAs would carry compliance costs. The bill's findings acknowledge CRAs face real legal and operational burdens, but on balance the bill was written to correct documented market failures, not to add costs for their own sake.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never advanced; no committee vote, no floor vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Maxine Waters introduced H.R. 3755 on September 13, 2017, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, where she was the ranking Democrat.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it died in committee at the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019, without a markup, a floor vote, or any Senate companion moving.
The bill had 34 cosponsors, all Democrats, giving it no Republican support to push it past committee leadership.

The bill's own findings cataloged years of Consumer Bureau enforcement and studies documenting credit bureau failures, including 2017 fines against Equifax, TransUnion, and Experian for deceptive marketing, yet no committee action followed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The credit bureaus, debt collectors, and lenders who would have faced new accuracy duties, fee caps, and lost revenue from credit-check and credit-score products kept the status quo; consumers with credit report errors got no relief from Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus, collectors, and scoring firms

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.role: U.S. Representative (CA-43), sponsor and Ranking Member of the House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 13, 2017, drafting a comprehensive rewrite of the Fair Credit Reporting Act.

against.name: Financial Services Committee Republicans and industry
against.role: Committee majority and affected credit and lending industries
against.what_they_did: No hearing or markup of the bill was scheduled during the 115th Congress, leaving it without a path to a floor vote.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; it never left the committee for the full 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was the top Democrat on the Financial Services Committee; no Republican support appears in the record, and the Republican-led committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill overhauls their dispute process, adds appeal rights and injunctive relief for consumers, requires free scores and freezes, bans deceptive marketing and promotional auto-renewals, and lets the CFPB cap fees on the consumer products they sell. The bill's findings document CFPB fines against all three for deceiving consumers about credit scores and subscription traps.

The bill shortens how long collections can appear on reports, mandates removal of paid or settled debts, restricts medical collections (half of all collection trade lines), and requires furnishers to keep records substantiating disputes.

industries.industry: Employers using credit checks in hiring
industries.note: Title II bans the use of credit information in most employment decisions, removing a screening tool the bill's findings show is used by a growing share of employers despite little evidence it predicts performance.

industries.industry: Private student lenders and for-profit colleges
industries.note: Delinquent private education loan marks would be removed for borrowers who show repayment history, and victims of school fraud would get credit relief, but the bill does not touch the loans themselves.

The CFPB would gain authority to oversee how credit scoring models are developed and to require study of newer and alternative scoring models at Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, tightening oversight of a concentrated industry without banning it.
